length.description: Maximum characters. Omitted means unlimited, which behaves exactly like text.

numeric_precision.description: Total significant digits. Omitted means an unconstrained numeric.

numeric_scale.description: Digits kept right of the decimal point; requires precision. Negative rounds left of the point.

nullable.description: Whether the field accepts null. A constraint on a field of any type, never a type itself; false emits NOT NULL.

collation.description: Collation driving comparison and ordering; defaults to the database collation.

fractional_seconds.description: Fractional-second digits retained by time, timetz, timestamp, timestamptz and interval; values beyond it are rounded.

column.description: Placeholder in postgres.check, replaced with the quoted column name when the constraint is emitted.

string.description: Single-line text where a length bound is meaningful: names, titles, labels. Prefer text when there is no maximum, and enum when the values form a closed set.

html.note: Set maxlength from the length attribute.

postgres.note: varchar and text are the same storage; the length is a constraint, not an optimization.

text.description: Unbounded prose: article bodies, comments, logs. Prefer string when a length limit is part of the contract.

boolean.description: A true/false fact: flags, toggles, switches. Prefer enum if a third state could ever appear, rather than a nullable boolean.

html.note: An unchecked box submits nothing; map absence to false.

int32.description: The general-purpose signed integer: counts, quantities, offsets. Prefer int64 for identifiers or anything that can outgrow two billion.

int64.description: Signed 64-bit integers: database keys, byte sizes, high-resolution counters. Values beyond 2^53 lose precision as JSON numbers, so they travel as strings; storage is still a native 64-bit integer.

html.note: Not type="number": browsers parse it as a double and lose digits past 2^53. Keep it a string in JS (BigInt for math).

float64.description: The default floating-point number: measurements, ratios, scores. Never money or exact quantities - use decimal for anything where digits must be exact.

postgres.note: float(p) with p in 25-53 is a spelling of double precision.

decimal.description: Exact decimal value represented as text. Use for money, rates, quantities, and other values where decimal precision must be preserved. Precision and scale are determined by the target system.

html.note: Not type="number": that converts through a binary float. Keep it a string in JS; use a decimal library for math.

postgres.note: Exact arithmetic. Without precision and scale it stores any value as given.

object.description: A nested JSON object: structured payloads, settings blobs, documents. Prefer dedicated fields or columns once the shape is stable enough to query.

html.note: No native JSON input; parse with JSON.parse before submit or use a structured editor.

postgres.note: json keeps the input text and key order verbatim; jsonb normalizes it and is the indexable one.

array.description: An ordered JSON list: tags, attachments, embedded collections. Prefer a separate table or repeated field when elements need identity or independent querying.

html.note: No native JSON input; parse with JSON.parse before submit or use a structured editor.

postgres.note: A native array (text[]) is the alternative when every element shares one scalar type.

enum.description: One value from a closed, named set: statuses, roles, kinds. Prefer string for open-ended sets and boolean for exactly two states.

html.note: Options come from the declared labels; use radio buttons when there are few.

postgres.note: Requires a named type created up front; Postgres rejects an inline unnamed enum.

name.description: Name of the generated enum type, unique per schema.

labels.description: Ordered labels; declaration order is the sort order. Labels can be added later, never removed.

any.description: Deliberately unconstrained: passthrough payloads and escape hatches. Reach for it last - every consumer inherits the validation burden.

html.note: No native JSON input; parse with JSON.parse before submit or use a structured editor.

date.description: A calendar date with no time or zone: birthdays, due dates, effective dates. Prefer date_time for an actual instant.

time_local.standard: OpenAPI Format Registry (RFC 3339 partial-time, no offset)
time_local.description: A wall-clock time with no offset: daily schedules like 'every day at 14:30' that follow whatever zone applies. Pair with timezone when the zone is fixed.

html.note: step="1" shows seconds; without it browsers submit HH:MM, which the pattern rejects - append ":00".

postgres.note: Plain time drops the offset, which is exactly what makes it the local variant.

date_time.description: An absolute instant with offset - the default for created/updated timestamps and anything that really happened. Prefer date_time_local only for deliberately floating times.

html.note: No native input for an instant. datetime-local yields a wall-clock time; combine it with the user's zone (Intl.DateTimeFormat().resolvedOptions().timeZone) and convert to an offset or Z before sending.

postgres.note: Stored as UTC and rendered in the session TimeZone; timestamp keeps no offset at all.

date_time_local.standard: OpenAPI Format Registry (RFC 3339 date-time with no offset)
date_time_local.description: A date and time with no offset: floating events like 'Jan 1 at midnight, wherever the user is'. Prefer date_time for real instants; pair with timezone to reconstruct one.

html.note: Exact match; browsers submit HH:MM without seconds unless step is set - append ":00" if absent.

postgres.note: timestamp keeps no offset at all; it names a wall clock, not an instant.

duration.description: A span of time (ISO 8601): timeouts, retention windows, billing periods. A length, not a position - prefer date_time for points in time.

html.note: No native duration input; usually rendered as separate number fields and assembled into ISO 8601.

postgres.note: Three independent components (months, days, microseconds) that never normalize into each other.

fields.description: Restricts which units are stored; omitted keeps every field.

timezone.description: An IANA zone name like America/New_York: user preferences and scheduling context. Store the name, never a raw offset - offsets change with DST and law.

postgres.note: No native zone type; store the IANA name and validate against pg_timezone_names.

email.description: An email address: login and contact fields. Accepting internationalized mailboxes is a validation choice, not a separate type.

postgres.note: The citext extension gives case-insensitive comparison without a lower() index.

hostname.description: A DNS hostname: servers and endpoints without scheme or path. Prefer uri when a full locator travels; internationalized names are a validation choice.

ipv4.description: A dotted-quad IPv4 host address. Prefer cidr for networks rather than hosts.

postgres.note: inet holds a host with an optional netmask; use cidr when the value is a network.

ipv6.description: An IPv6 host address. Prefer cidr for prefixes rather than hosts.

postgres.note: One inet column stores both families; the address itself carries the version.

cidr.description: A network prefix of either IP family: allowlists, routing rules. Prefer ipv4 or ipv6 for a single host.

postgres.note: Rejects any bit set to the right of the netmask, which inet accepts.

uri.description: An absolute URI with scheme: links, webhooks, resource locators. Use string for relative paths.

uuid.description: A 128-bit universal identifier, any version: primary keys and references. Which version to mint (such as time-ordered v7) is a generation option, not a separate type.

html.note: Usually generated (crypto.randomUUID()) and shown read-only rather than typed.

postgres.note: Stored as 16 bytes regardless of the input spelling.

phone.description: An E.164 phone number (+country code, digits only): dialing and SMS. Store normalized; display formatting is presentation, not data.

html.note: Users type local formats; normalize to E.164 before submit (e.g. libphonenumber-js).

binary.standard: OpenAPI 3.2 binary data / RFC 4648 Section 4 (base64 in JSON)
binary.description: Raw bytes: file uploads, blobs, digests. Inside JSON they travel as standard base64 (RFC 4648); storage keeps the decoded bytes.

html.note: Encode the file's bytes to base64 for JSON, or send multipart/form-data and skip the encoding.

postgres.note: Variable length with no fixed-size form; large payloads can move to a large object instead.

secret.standard: OpenAPI Format Registry (display hint only, not a guarantee)
secret.description: Sensitive text that must never be displayed or logged: passwords, API keys. The format is a masking hint, not protection - hash or encrypt at rest.

html.note: Use autocomplete="new-password" or "current-password" for user passwords so password managers engage; "off" for API keys and tokens.

postgres.note: The type offers no protection; encrypt with pgcrypto or keep the value out of the database.

media_type.description: A concrete media type like application/json: labeling stored content.

slug.description: A lowercase-hyphen URL token (getting-started): readable path segments derived from a title. Presentation identity only - prefer uuid as the real key.

html.note: Usually derived from a title: lowercase, NFKD-strip accents, replace runs of non [a-z0-9] with '-', trim '-'.

country.description: An ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code (US): the interchange default for countries.

postgres.note: char(2) fits but blank-pads and compares by the padded value; text avoids that.

currency.description: An ISO 4217 currency code (USD): pair it with a decimal amount to represent money. Never derive it from country or locale - people transact across borders.

locale.description: A BCP 47 language tag (en, en-US): a language with optional script and region, for formatting, translations, and user preferences.

color.standard: CSS Color Module Level 4 (hex notation), canonical lowercase
color.description: An sRGB color as lowercase #rrggbb or #rrggbbaa - the exact form <input type="color"> produces, so it round-trips through forms, JSON, JS/TS and SQL unchanged. Prefer css_color only for wide-gamut or design-token values.

html.note: The picker returns lowercase #rrggbb; #rrggbbaa needs the newer alpha attribute where supported, else a separate opacity input.

char.description: Exactly one character: a grade, flag, or single-letter code. Prefer string for anything that can grow, and enum when the values form a closed set.

postgres.note: Bare char is char(1); the blank-padding that makes char awkward needs a length above 1.

int8.description: Tiny signed integers (-128..127) where the bound is part of the contract. Prefer int32 as the general-purpose default.

postgres.note: Postgres has no 1-byte integer; smallint is the narrowest signed type.

int16.description: Signed 16-bit integers: compact numeric codes and small bounded quantities. Prefer int32 as the general-purpose default.

uint8.description: Unsigned bytes (0..255): color channels, small numeric codes. Prefer int32 unless the byte range is intrinsic to the data.

postgres.note: Postgres has no unsigned integers; smallint covers the whole uint8 range.

uint16.description: Unsigned 16-bit integers (0..65535). Prefer port for network ports specifically, and int32 when a negative value could ever appear.

postgres.note: No unsigned integers; integer covers the whole uint16 range.

uint32.description: Unsigned 32-bit integers: large counters and IDs from systems that use them. Prefer int64 in new designs; signed types survive arithmetic and language boundaries better.

postgres.note: Postgres has no unsigned integers; bigint covers the whole uint32 range.

uint64.description: The full unsigned 64-bit range: hashes and foreign systems' identifiers. Most languages and JSON cannot represent the upper half natively, so values travel as strings; prefer int64 unless the source really uses all 64 bits.

html.note: Not type="number": browsers parse it as a double and lose digits past 2^53. Keep it a string in JS (BigInt for math).

postgres.note: No unsigned 64-bit type; numeric(20, 0) covers the whole uint64 range.

double_int.standard: OpenAPI Format Registry (integer exactly representable as a double)
double_int.description: Integers exactly representable in an IEEE double (up to 2^53-1): safe as a plain number for every JSON consumer, including JavaScript. Prefer int64 when the full 64-bit range matters and consumers accept strings.

postgres.note: Bounded by 2^53, so it always survives a round trip through a double.

float32.description: Single-precision floats: bulk sensor readings or ML weights where memory beats precision. Prefer float64 as the default floating-point type.

postgres.note: float(p) with p in 1-24 is a spelling of real; it is not a stored precision.

decimal128.description: IEEE 754 decimal128: exact decimals with a defined 34-significant-digit width, for interchange with fixed-width financial systems. Prefer decimal when arbitrary precision is acceptable.

html.note: Not type="number": that converts through a binary float. Keep it a string in JS; use a decimal library for math.

postgres.note: 34 significant decimal digits, which numeric holds exactly and a float does not.

time.description: A wall-clock time with an explicit UTC offset. Prefer time_local for schedules that float with the local zone.

html.note: The time input has no offset; append the user's current UTC offset before sending.

postgres.note: timetz stores a fixed UTC offset, not a zone; plain time drops the offset.

unix_time.standard: POSIX.1-2024 (IEEE Std 1003.1-2024) seconds since the Epoch
unix_time.description: Seconds since the Unix epoch as an integer: compact machine timestamps and TTLs. Prefer date_time for anything humans or APIs read directly.

html.note: Show as a local date-time and convert: Math.floor(new Date(value).getTime() / 1000).

idn_email.description: An internationalized email address: non-ASCII local parts and domains. Prefer email when every consumer requires ASCII.

html.note: Not type="email": browsers reject non-ASCII local parts there.

idn_hostname.description: An internationalized (IDNA2008) hostname. Prefer hostname when values are guaranteed ASCII or already punycode-encoded.

ipv4_cidr.description: An IPv4 network prefix like 192.0.2.0/24. Prefer cidr when either family may appear, and ipv4 for a single host.

postgres.note: Rejects any bit set to the right of the netmask, which inet accepts.

ipv6_cidr.description: An IPv6 network prefix like 2001:db8::/32. Prefer cidr when either family may appear, and ipv6 for a single host.

postgres.note: One cidr column stores both families; the prefix itself carries the version.

mac_address.description: An EUI-48 hardware address: device inventory, DHCP leases. Never an identity for people or accounts - MACs are spoofable and privacy-sensitive.

postgres.note: macaddr is EUI-48; macaddr8 is the EUI-64 variant.

uri_reference.description: A URI reference, absolute or relative: redirect targets, in-site paths. Prefer uri when an absolute, scheme-carrying value is required.

iri.description: An internationalized absolute URI: user-facing links in any script, unencoded. Prefer uri when consumers require ASCII with percent-encoding.

html.note: Not type="url": it normalizes non-ASCII to punycode/percent-encoding.

iri_reference.description: An internationalized URI reference, absolute or relative. Prefer iri for absolute-only values and uri_reference for ASCII-only ones.

uuid_v7.description: A time-ordered UUID: new primary keys that index and sort by creation time. Prefer uuid when accepting identifiers you did not mint.

html.note: Generated server-side, shown read-only.

postgres.note: Same storage as any UUID; the time ordering is a property of the value, not the type.

ulid.description: A lexically sortable 128-bit ID in Crockford Base32: time-ordered keys that stay readable as text. Prefer uuid_v7 where native UUID column types and tooling matter.

html.note: Generated, shown read-only.

postgres.note: 128-bit like a UUID; storable as uuid if the Crockford base32 form is converted on the way in.

base64.description: Binary content as standard base64 text: payloads embedded in JSON. Prefer binary for raw transport and base64url when the value travels in URLs or filenames.

html.note: Read the file and encode it (FileReader.readAsDataURL, then strip the data: prefix).

postgres.note: Stored decoded, not as the base64 text; bytea_output picks hex or escape on the way out.

base64url.description: URL-safe base64 (no + or /): tokens and digests placed in URLs. Prefer base64 for ordinary embedded payloads.

html.note: Encode as base64, then replace + with -, / with _ and drop padding.

postgres.note: Same bytes as base64; only the transport alphabet differs.

css_color.description: Any single CSS Color 4 value: hex, named, rgb(), hsl(), hwb(), lab(), lch(), oklab(), oklch() or color(display-p3 ...). The pattern only checks the shape; validate for real with CSS.supports('color', value). Level 5 expressions (color-mix(), relative colors, light-dark(), var()) are computed in context and are deliberately not data.

html.note: Validate with CSS.supports('color', value); pair with <input type="color"> only when the value is sRGB hex.

commonmark.description: Markdown (CommonMark) source: user-authored rich content stored as written. Prefer html for already-rendered markup and text for plain prose.

html.note: Pair with a rendered preview; sanitize the rendered HTML.

postgres.note: Markdown source; Postgres stores the text and never parses it.

html.description: HTML markup stored as-is: rendered output, email bodies. Sanitize on the way in; prefer commonmark when users author the content.

html.note: Sanitize (e.g. DOMPurify) before rendering; never assign untrusted input to innerHTML.

postgres.note: Markup source; escape it on output, not on the way in.

json_pointer.description: An absolute JSON Pointer (/users/0/email): addressing a location inside a document from its root.

relative_json_pointer.description: A JSON Pointer relative to a known position (1/name). Prefer json_pointer when addressing from the document root.

postgres.note: Resolved against a base pointer; the leading integer counts levels up.

uri_template.description: An RFC 6570 URL pattern with {variables}: route and link templates. Prefer uri for concrete, already-expanded links.

regex.description: An ECMA-262 regular expression source: validation rules and matchers stored as data. Prefer enum when the acceptable values are simply a closed set.

semver.description: A Semantic Version (1.4.2-rc.1): package and API versions with defined precedence. Prefer string for version-ish labels that do not follow SemVer.

postgres.note: Ordering is lexical unless the parts are split out or an extension type is used.

jwt.description: A compact JSON Web Token: signed claims passed between parties. Handle like secret in storage and logs; prefer secret for opaque credentials.

sha256.description: A SHA-256 digest: content addressing, integrity checks, dedup keys. Never for passwords - those take a dedicated password hash stored as secret.

html.note: Computed (crypto.subtle.digest('SHA-256', bytes)), shown read-only.

postgres.note: 32 decoded bytes; bytea has no fixed-length form, so length is enforced by a check.

port.description: A TCP/UDP port number (0..65535): service endpoints and configuration. Prefer uint16 for 16-bit values that are not ports.

postgres.note: No unsigned 16-bit type; integer plus a range check covers 0-65535.

cron.description: A POSIX crontab expression (0 3 * * *): recurring schedules. Prefer duration for simple intervals and date_time for one-shot schedules.

country_alpha3.description: An ISO 3166-1 alpha-3 country code (USA): feeds and standards that require three letters. Prefer country (alpha-2) as the default.

html.note: Intl has no alpha-3 list; map from alpha-2 with a lookup table.

subdivision.description: An ISO 3166-2 subdivision code (US-CA): states, provinces, regions. Carries its country prefix, so no separate country field is needed to interpret it.

language.description: An ISO 639 language code (en): tagging what language content is in. Prefer locale when region or script variants matter.

http_date.description: The HTTP header date format (IMF-fixdate): Last-Modified, Expires, and friends. HTTP interchange only - prefer date_time everywhere else.

html.note: Not entered by people; format with new Date(value).toUTCString().

postgres.note: A header wire format, parsed to an instant on the way in. The OpenAPI registry still sources it to RFC 7231, which RFC 9110 obsoletes.

wikidata_qid.description: A Wikidata entity ID (Q42): linking records to globally known entities. Prefer the domain registry when one exists - doi, orcid, lei, isbn.

doi.description: A Digital Object Identifier: citations to papers, datasets, publications. Prefer uri only for links that are not registered DOIs.

orcid.description: An ORCID iD identifying a researcher. Prefer lei for organizations and wikidata_qid for entities outside scholarly identity.

lei.description: A Legal Entity Identifier: organizations in financial and regulatory contexts. Identity, not routing - prefer bic for payment routing.

media_range.description: An HTTP media range with wildcards and parameters: Accept-style negotiation. Prefer media_type for one concrete type.

postgres.note: A range admits wildcards and parameters; media_type admits neither.

sf_integer.description: An HTTP Structured Fields integer (15 digits max): numeric members of structured headers. Prefer int64 outside header serialization.

postgres.note: Structured Fields caps integers at fifteen digits, well inside bigint.

sf_decimal.description: An HTTP Structured Fields decimal (three fractional digits): weights and q-values in headers. Prefer decimal outside header serialization.

postgres.note: At most twelve integer and three fractional digits, which numeric keeps exactly.

sf_string.description: An HTTP Structured Fields quoted string (printable ASCII): textual members of structured headers. Prefer string outside header serialization.

postgres.note: Printable ASCII only; DQUOTE and backslash are escaped in transport.

sf_token.description: An HTTP Structured Fields token like gzip: short symbolic header values. Prefer enum for closed sets outside HTTP.

postgres.note: A bare token, never quoted; that is what distinguishes it from sf_string.

sf_binary.description: An HTTP Structured Fields byte sequence (colon-delimited base64): binary members of structured headers. Prefer base64 outside header serialization.

postgres.note: Stored decoded; the surrounding colons are Structured Fields syntax, not data.

sf_boolean.description: An HTTP Structured Fields boolean (?1 / ?0): flags in structured headers. Prefer boolean outside header serialization.

postgres.note: Serialized as ?1 and ?0 on the wire, which is syntax rather than a distinct type.

iban.description: An International Bank Account Number: identifying accounts for payments. Pair with bic for cross-border routing and treat as sensitive data.

html.note: Users type it in groups of four; strip spaces and uppercase before submit, then verify the mod-97 checksum.

bic.description: A BIC/SWIFT code identifying a bank for payment routing. Routing, not identity - prefer lei to identify the legal entity itself.

isbn.description: An ISBN identifying a book edition. Prefer gtin for general retail products; every ISBN-13 is a GTIN, but not the reverse.

html.note: Strip hyphens and spaces before submit; the check digit needs code, not a pattern.

gtin.description: A GS1 GTIN (UPC/EAN family) identifying a retail product. Prefer isbn when the domain is specifically books.

html.note: Usually scanned; the check digit needs code, not a pattern.
